walkthroughs.body_html:
The Changing Economic World — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Changing Economic World brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Changing Economic World.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative data?
options: Gentrification means evicting all residents by force.
Quantitative data is always more scientific and reliable than qualitative.
Quantitative data is numerical and measurable (traffic counts, river width); qualitative data is descriptive and non-numerical (interview quotes, photo descriptions, field sketches).
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.

mcqs.q: What is the main social impact of gentrification?
options: Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.
Displacement of long-term lower-income residents as rents and property prices rise, often along with loss of community businesses and cultural identity — even if the area looks 'improved'.
Gentrification means evicting all residents by force.
Gentrification only has positive effects because it makes areas nicer.

mcqs.q: Why do meanders migrate across a floodplain?
options: Faster water on the outside of the bend causes erosion (river cliff); slower water on the inside causes deposition (slip-off slope) — over time the channel shifts laterally.
Meanders form because rivers flow around obstacles like rocks.
Meanders form because the river is going downhill very steeply.
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.
